– like addresses and corporate filings – are vital. They add context that strengthens risk assessments and reveals hidden links.
The question "is this the same entity?". Answered by a registry identifier or by a filing naming both as one.
No public IRS register among the sources cited; taken from a filing that states it
4.2 Filings that establish identity.

A registry identifier retrieved from the issuing body's own system (the Global LEI Index, EDGAR, BrokerCheck or IAPD, SIRENE, the Companies House register), or from a filing on a regulator's system that states it, has origin REGULATORY_PUBLIC_RECORD and derivation OBSERVED.
a filing or registry record names both as one entity (4.2).

Every merge records the surviving record, the absorbed record, the identifier or filing that justified it, the actor and the date. The absorbed record's identifier is kept and resolves to the surviving record. A merge with no recorded justifying identifier or filing is a defect. Any merge can be undone: the unmerge restores both records, and each claim returns to the record its evidence supports.
Filing or registry record naming both as one entity, or listing both identifiers as one filer's own
Kept separate, not merged; identity only if a register or filing links both to one entity
If evidence shows a merge was wrong (for example a filing showing two distinct entities behind one identifier assignment), the merge is reversed under 5.9 and the reason is recorded.

Private family entities, foreign entities outside accessible registers and informal groups may carry none. Their records are kept separate, related where evidence supports it, and merged only when an identifier or naming filing appears. The correct number of merges without such evidence is zero.

Where an identifier identifies a tax account or a filer rather than a legal entity, a shared identifier establishes that the records share that account or filer. Identity of the legal entities then needs an identifier of legal-entity scope or a naming filing.
Rebrands without a filing.

Classic probabilistic record linkage accepts pairs in the upper weight band as links (Fellegi and Sunter, 1969). This methodology does not: it merges only on registry identifiers or naming filings, keeps every merge reversible, and records all other connections as typed, dated and sourced relations.
Internal Revenue Service, Rev. 2-2014 (the revision hosted at irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf and linked from the IRS EIN page, reviewed 2026-07-17)

手順・やり方.quote: This article will explore the two most important assets in entity resolution – primary and secondary identifiers. It will cover their differences, their importance, and best practices for using them in an entity resolution framework.

Entity resolution is the method of determining when different records from one or more data sources refer to the same entity. In a corporate context, these entities could be companies, businesses, or other organisations. Entity resolution helps organisations:
Entity resolution addresses these risks. It uses strong data matching and classification methods. At the heart of these procedures lie
: Assign match confidence scores based on how many primary and secondary identifiers match. This approach ensures a risk-based method, where higher-risk entities face deeper checks.

Wrongly merging two entities is costly and hard to detect: claims from both are mixed and the distinction is lost. A missed merge leaves a duplicate that can be labelled and merged later. This methodology accepts more duplicates in exchange for fewer false merges. Measures of resolution quality therefore report false merges and missed merges separately; see
Temporal Data & Freshness Methodology

The foundation of probabilistic record linkage: m and u probabilities, agreement weights and the three decision bands. This methodology uses the model to rank candidates and differs in not accepting any band as a merge.

The LEI is a 20-character code under ISO 17442; each legal entity is assigned a single LEI and each LEI represents only one entity. Level 1 data records who is who; Level 2 data records who owns whom (direct and ultimate parents). This methodology treats Level 1 as identity evidence and Level 2 as relation evidence.
. UK company number: Companies Act 2006, section 1066; Companies House. Each body defines the scope of its own identifier; this methodology uses each only within that scope.
Where this methodology differs from common practice.
